newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian rules on telecom sale may repel foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Russian rules on telecom sale may repel foreigners.

text.p: Russia's decision to bar foreign strategic investors from its Svyazinvest telecoms holding company is bad news for the company and makes it less attractive to portfolio investors, telecoms analysts said on Thursday.

They said foreign investors were not set to see particularly high returns on the stake in the absence of a western strategic investor with control over how the firm is run. A strategic investor could also inject fresh capital.

"Svyazinvest will probably appreciate with the development of the market, but the margin of appreciation cannot be as attractive as that in some of the underlying telecoms," said Alfa Capital telecoms analyst Kristen Burton Steiner.
Russia plans to sell a 25 percent stake in Svyazinvest to foreign portfolio investors and 24 percent to domestic buyers, Communications Minister Vladimir Bulgak said on Wednesday.
But an analyst at a Russian investment bank said Svyazinvest's finances and the legal situation regarding its ownership of stakes in regional telecoms were unclear.
"That is even more important to portfolio investors than to strategic investors," he said.
He said foreign communications companies who had already shown interest in Svyazinvest, which holds stakes in 85 regional telecoms, would see less advantage in being a portfolio investor.
Bulgak told a news conference that the 25 percent stake for foreigners would not go to a single investor.
"If a strategic investor receives 25 percent and one share, he could influence the security of the country," he said.
Italy's Stet SpA won a 1995 auction for a 25 percent Svyazinvest stake, but the deal fell through.
Burton Steiner said Svyazinvest needed the direction and experience of a foreign telecommunications company in order to put together and carry out a strategic vision.
"They don't have the know-how. They need a Western international telecoms provider to give direction," she said.
AT&T, US West, Ericsson and other major telecommunications companies have said in the past that they would consider a stratetic investment in Svyazinvest.
But Svyazinvest could lose out from the new sale plan, details of which have not been released, since a sale to portfolio investors would not guarantee investment funds.
About $730 million of the $1.3 billion price for Svyazinvest in the failed Stet deal was for investment in the company.
"Much of the (new) sale proceeds are earmarked for the federal budget," the Russian bank telecoms analyst said.

Svyazinvest was not expected to gain a marked financial advantage from acquisition of a controlling stake in Russian international long-distance telephone company Rostelekom, which the government is transferring to Svyazinvest.
Rostelekom, a leader on the Russian equities market, has said it would be virtually unaffected by the move, and that no merger of the companies was in the works.
"Rostelekom is not going to kick in any money if it doesn't have to," Burton Steiner said.
